guideTitle: 7 Best Electric Snow Shovels Under $150 in 2026
metaTitle: Best Electric Snow Shovels Under $150 in 2026
metaDescription: Seven corded and cordless electric snow shovels compared for light snow on steps, decks and short driveways, with notes on batteries, width and throw distance.
introParagraphs: An electric snow shovel sits in an interesting gap between a plain shovel and a full snow blower. It is far lighter than a gas machine, needs no pull cord and stores on a hook in the garage, yet it throws snow rather than making you lift it. For a porch, a set of steps or a short driveway after a modest snowfall, that middle ground is exactly right.

At this budget the choice splits into two camps. Two corded models plug into an outdoor outlet and never run out of power, while five cordless models trade that endless runtime for freedom from an extension cord. Both camps clear a path about 10 to 14 inches wide and a few inches deep, which is enough for light and medium snow but not for a deep, wet blizzard.

We evaluated these from their published specs and buyer feedback, not hands-on testing. Check the width and depth against your usual snowfall, and be honest about how much snow you move per storm. The best shovel for a quick walkway clear is not the best one for a long driveway, and the cons below reflect that.

products.name: Yardzpo 14 Inch Cordless Snow Shovel with 2 Batteries
products.description:
The Yardzpo is the most capable cordless shovel in this price tier on paper. A 14 inch clearing width fits typical sidewalks, driveways and steps, and an 830W all-copper motor spins up to 16,000 RPM. Two batteries come in the box, with the listing citing more than 50 minutes of runtime, so you can swap and keep moving through a longer clear.

The adjustable deflector sends snow to the front, left at 45 degrees or right, and a 33 foot throw distance is the longest of any model here. An LED display gives you status while you work. The cost is that this is a large tool for the money, and the listing leaves out a few details worth checking, such as exact weight and included accessories.

Compared with the SKIL at 10 inches, it covers more ground per pass. Compared with the Steelite at 13 inches, it throws farther and adds directional control. Compared with the corded Westinghouse, it removes the cord, though the Westinghouse never runs out of power. It is the best fit for a driveway-length clear.

products.name: Steelite 20V Cordless Electric Snow Shovel, 13 Inch
products.description:
The Steelite gives you two 20V 4.0Ah batteries, which is the most generous battery package among the 20V models here. The listing claims it clears 300 pounds of snow per minute at a 13 inch width and 6 inch depth, and a chute that adjusts 30 degrees each way lets you aim the throw up to 23 feet.

Having a spare battery already in the box is the practical win. A single battery can empty before a long driveway is done, and a swap turns that into a short pause instead of waiting for a recharge. The drawback is that it is a less familiar brand, so confirm return terms and support before you buy.

Compared with the SKIL, which brings one 4.0Ah battery and a 10 inch blade, the Steelite offers a wider path and a second battery. Compared with the Yardzpo, it has a shorter throw and no stated copper motor. It suits households that want a straightforward cordless tool with spare power.

products.name: VOLTASK 24V Cordless Snow Shovel, 13.2 Inch
products.description:
The VOLTASK is easy to maneuver without feeling like a toy. A 13.2 inch blade clears paths up to about 13 inches wide, and a 24V 4.0Ah battery supplies about 30 minutes of continuous runtime, enough for steps, a deck and a short driveway. The ergonomic handle is designed to reduce strain, and dual safety switches prevent the motor from starting by accident.

It lacks some of the extras found on pricier models, such as a second battery in the box or a wide directional range. Confirm the current specs and what is included on the listing before buying, since bundles vary. The single battery means plan your clear in one session.

Compared with the Pavrxeo, it throws farther at 23 feet and has a wider blade, though the Pavrxeo digs deeper per pass. Compared with the Steelite, it comes with one battery rather than two. It is a good fit for people who value a comfortable grip and a safe start over the longest possible runtime.

products.name: Pavrxeo 21V Cordless Snow Shovel, 13 Inch

specList.label: Storage
specList.value: Collapses flat with a knob twist

products.description:
The Pavrxeo is built for garages where every square foot counts. A knob twist collapses the frame so it stores flat, ending the usual shuffle of leaning a long tool against a wall. A built-in shock-absorbing system in the handle is meant to reduce jolts that travel into your back.

It cuts a 12 inch wide, 7 inch deep path per pass, and the listing claims that is 40 percent more depth than lighter models. That extra depth is the point if your snowfalls are a little heavier. The listing is thin on other numbers such as throw distance and battery capacity, so check the page for those details before ordering.

Compared with the VOLTASK 13.2, it digs deeper but we have less information on throw. Compared with the SKIL, it is wider and better for slightly deeper snow. It is the right pick when storage and back comfort matter as much as power.

products.name: SKIL PWR CORE 20 10 Inch Snow Shovel Kit

specList.label: Driveway claim
specList.value: 3 inches on a 1-car driveway per charge

products.description:
The SKIL kit includes everything: the 20V snow shovel, a 4.0Ah battery and a 60W charger. The maker states that a single charge clears up to 3 inches of snow from a one-car driveway, and the shovel throws snow up to 20 feet. For decks, patios and walkways it is a neat, ready-to-use package from an established tool brand.

The 10 inch blade is the narrowest here, so a wide driveway takes more passes. It lacks some of the extras found on pricier models, and the single battery means you plan the clear in one go. Confirm the current specs and contents on the listing, because kits can change.

Compared with the Steelite at 13 inches and two batteries, the SKIL is narrower but comes from a more familiar name. Compared with the Westinghouse corded model, it frees you from a cord but cannot run all day. It fits people who already own SKIL batteries or want a trusted brand for light snow.

products.name: Westinghouse WSnow11S 11 Inch Corded Snow Shovel
products.description:
The Westinghouse does something no battery model can: it never runs out. A 120V 10A corded motor throws 300 pounds of snow per minute, clearing an 11 inch wide path that is 6 inches deep, with a throw of 20 feet. The listing calls it lightweight and easy to maneuver, and it suits driveways, sidewalks, walkways and porches.

The cost of unlimited runtime is the cord. You need an outdoor-rated extension cord within reach of an outlet, and you steer around it as you work. That limits range and adds a trip hazard, so it is best for small areas close to the house.

Compared with the Snow Joe 324E, it has an almost identical cord-based approach but a plainer feature list. Compared with the cordless models, it never needs charging, which matters if your battery always seems empty. Choose it for short, close-to-the-house clears where a cord is no hassle.

products.name: Snow Joe 324E Electric Snow Shovel with LED Headlight
products.description:
The Snow Joe 324E is the corded model with a headlight. A 10 amp motor moves up to 300 pounds of snow per minute, and a back-saving handle plus a lightweight body of about 14 pounds keep lifting to a minimum. The LED headlight lights the path for dawn and dusk clears, which is when most people shovel.

It requires no gas, no oil and no pull cords, so there is almost nothing to maintain. Like all corded tools it needs an extension cord, and the cord sets the working radius. The listing puts the clearing path at about 11 inches wide, so it is on the narrow side.

Compared with the Westinghouse, it adds the headlight and a back-friendly handle. Compared with the Yardzpo, it clears a narrower path and tethers you to an outlet, but it never needs a charge. Choose it for early-morning or evening clears of steps and short walkways.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Corded shovels run as long as there is power and weigh less than a battery model, but the cord limits range and gets in the way. Cordless shovels roam freely, but run out when the battery does. The Westinghouse WSnow11S and Snow Joe 324E are corded, while the Yardzpo, Steelite, VOLTASK, Pavrxeo and SKIL are cordless. If your clear is near an outlet, corded is simple and reliable.

Width decides how many passes you make, and depth decides whether the machine copes with a heavy snowfall. The Yardzpo clears 14 inches, the VOLTASK 13.2, the Steelite 13, the Pavrxeo 12 by 7 inches deep, the corded models 11 inches and the SKIL 10 inches. Wider is faster, deeper is safer for heavy snow. Think about your usual snowfall.

Battery size and count determine how much you can clear. The Steelite ships with two 4.0Ah batteries and the Yardzpo with two for 50+ minutes. The SKIL and VOLTASK each ship with one. If your clear takes longer than 30 minutes, a spare battery turns a frustrating stop into a quick swap.

A long throw keeps snow out of the path you just cleared, while a directional chute lets you aim away from cars and plants. The Yardzpo throws 33 feet with a three-way deflector, the VOLTASK and Steelite reach 23 feet and the Westinghouse and SKIL reach 20 feet. Pick based on how much room you have to dump snow.

Even a light shovel feels heavy after twenty minutes of pushing. Handle design matters as much as raw weight. The Snow Joe weighs about 14 pounds with a back-saving handle, the Pavrxeo adds a shock-absorbing handle and the VOLTASK has an ergonomic grip. Try to match the tool to your back.

A snow tool lives in the garage for nine months a year, so storage matters. The Pavrxeo folds flat with a knob twist, and the SKIL is described as compact to store. Others take a standing space. Measure before you buy if your garage is tight.

howWeEvaluated.title: Clearing power
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared width, depth and stated snow capacity. The Yardzpo at 14 inches led, followed by the VOLTASK, Steelite and Pavrxeo, while the SKIL at 10 inches trailed. Capacity claims such as 300 pounds per minute were noted but not tested.

howWeEvaluated.title: Runtime and power source
howWeEvaluated.description: This category weighs battery count, capacity and the reliability of a corded supply. The Yardzpo and Steelite earned credit for two batteries, the corded models for unlimited runtime, and single-battery kits lost points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Handling and comfort
howWeEvaluated.description: Weight, handle shape and safety switches were considered. The Snow Joe at about 14 pounds and the Pavrxeo with a shock-absorbing handle did well, with the VOLTASK's dual safety switches adding points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Throw and control
howWeEvaluated.description: Throw distance and chute adjustment shape how well a shovel keeps snow out of your way. The Yardzpo's 33 foot throw and three-way discharge led. Models with no stated throw scored neutral.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value at this budget
howWeEvaluated.description: Since all seven sit under the cap, we asked what each delivers. The Yardzpo leads for total capability, the Steelite for batteries and the Westinghouse for simple, dependable power. These are editorial judgments, not field tests.

faq.q: Is an electric snow shovel enough for a driveway?
faq.a: For a short driveway with light to moderate snow, yes. The SKIL kit is rated for 3 inches on a one-car driveway on a single charge, and the Yardzpo adds a second battery. Bigger driveways or deep snow call for a snow blower.

faq.q: Do I need a spare battery?
faq.a: If your clear takes more than 30 minutes, yes. The Steelite and Yardzpo include two batteries, while the VOLTASK lists about 30 minutes from one. A spare turns a stop into a quick swap.

faq.q: Are corded shovels better in the cold?
faq.a: Often, yes, because batteries lose capacity in deep cold. The Westinghouse and Snow Joe draw power from the outlet, so cold does not shorten the runtime. You still manage a cord on icy ground.

faq.q: Can they handle wet, heavy snow?
faq.a: Not well. These tools are best on light to moderate snow, and wet snow strains the motor. Take shallow passes, and consider a larger machine if wet snow is common.
The Snow Joe 324E lists about 14 pounds, and the VOLTASK is also easy to maneuver. Weights for others are not always stated on the listings. Check the product page if weight matters.

faq.q: How far do they throw snow?
faq.a: The Yardzpo is claimed to throw up to 33 feet, the VOLTASK and Steelite up to 23 feet and the Westinghouse and SKIL up to 20 feet. Throw distance depends on snow weight and wind.

faq.q: How should I store the batteries?
faq.a: Keep them indoors at room temperature and charge them before the storm. Cold garages reduce runtime and slow charging. Never leave a battery in a freezing car.
